analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress from insider trading and puts their stock trades and financial records online for the public.
analysis.headline: Congress passed and the President signed the STOCK Act in April 2012, banning members from trading on nonpublic government information, by lopsided votes of 96-3 in the Senate and 417-2 in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: Before this law, no statute clearly said members of Congress could be prosecuted for trading stocks on information they learned in office. The STOCK Act states plainly that they, and senior executive-branch officials and judges, are covered by federal insider-trading law. It also requires officials to report their trades over $1,000 within 30 to 45 days, posts those reports and members' financial disclosures on public websites, bars officials from getting special access to IPO shares, blocks Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives from collecting bonuses while those companies are under government conservatorship, and makes officials disclose negotiations for future private-sector jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors and the general public. Before this law, it was legally unclear whether members of Congress could be prosecuted for trading on information they learned from briefings, committee work, or staff knowledge — the same trading that would be a crime for anyone else. The law also puts members' and senior officials' financial disclosures online, so anyone can look up what their representatives own and trade without traveling to Washington.

how_it_helps.text: It declares that members of Congress and congressional employees are not exempt from the insider-trading laws, so they can be punished for trading stocks on information from their jobs.
It requires officials to report any stock, bond, or commodity trade over $1,000 within 30 to 45 days, so the public can see what officials are trading while they are still in office.
It puts members' financial disclosure forms online within 30 days of filing, where anyone can search and download them, instead of requiring a trip to a government office.

It bars covered officials from getting IPO shares on terms unavailable to ordinary investors, and blocks Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives from receiving bonuses while those companies are in government conservatorship.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, congressional staff, and senior executive-branch officials, who must now report their trades within weeks, disclose mortgages on their homes, and give up any claim of being above insider-trading law. IPO underwriters lose the practice of allocating hot shares to officials. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives lose bonuses during conservatorship.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and senior officials

drawbacks.text: The insider-trading provision largely restates existing securities law and declares members 'not exempt' from it, rather than creating an easily enforced new crime; proving that a member traded on a specific piece of nonpublic information remains difficult, so the practical deterrent is weaker than the public debate implied.

The Senate-passed version would have required political-intelligence consultants — firms that sell information gathered from congressional contacts to investors — to register and disclose as lobbyists; the final law stripped that out, leaving only a Comptroller General study of the political-intelligence business.

The final law dropped Title II of the Senate-passed bill, a package of expanded public-corruption penalties (including broader bribery definitions and longer sentences), so the corruption-prosecution reforms never became part of this law.
Trades in widely diversified mutual funds are exempt from the 30-45 day transaction reporting, so the disclosure requirement does not reach all forms of investing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: the law closes an embarrassing legal gap, lets the public see officials' trades within weeks, and bars officials from getting special IPO access. The drawbacks are serious on enforcement: the core prohibition restates existing securities law rather than creating a self-executing crime for legislators, leaving cases hard to bring, and the one provision that would have required the political-intelligence industry to register as lobbyists was dropped from the final bill. Honest supporters would also note that later Congresses scaled back parts of it, so the law's practical bite has been debated.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it by near-unanimous votes and the President signed it in April 2012, though the House version dropped a provision that would have forced political-intelligence consultants to register as lobbyists.

narrative.text: The Senate's first procedural vote on taking up the bill passed 93-2 on January 30, 2012, an unusually strong showing.
The Senate passed the bill 96-3 on February 2, 2012.
The House passed it 417-2 on February 9, 2012.
The final law was signed April 4, 2012, as Public Law 112-105.

The Senate version had included a requirement that political-intelligence consultants register under lobbying-disclosure law; the House version replaced it with a Comptroller General study, and that weaker version is what became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary investors, who no longer compete against members of Congress trading on information gathered in office, and the public, which can now see officials' trades within weeks.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; political-intelligence firms partly escaped

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly unanimous in both chambers: Senate passage was 96-3 (50 Democrats and 44 Republicans voting yes) and House passage 417-2 (all 185 voting Democrats and 232 Republicans in favor).

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior federal officials (as a group)
industries.note: They give up the implicit assumption that trading on information learned in office carries no personal legal risk, must report trades within weeks, disclose home mortgages, and disclose job negotiations with private employers. The cost to them is compliance and legal exposure, not their salaries or wealth.

The Senate-passed bill would have made these firms register as lobbyists and disclose their clients; the final law only requires a government study of the industry, leaving its operations largely undisclosed. An industry built on selling officials' information to investors survived mostly intact.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac executives
industries.note: Senior executives of the mortgage-finance companies, which were in government conservatorship after the 2008 crisis, are barred from receiving bonuses while the companies remain under government control.
